title: Super funds on alert as credit cracks appear
full_text:
Major super funds are warning of deeper cracks appearing in Australia’s $200bn private credit market, parts of which are frozen in the wake of the Bathla Group collapse.
Billions of dollars of Australians’ super savings are tied up in privately dealt loans.
Bathla was tipped into administration last Tuesday, with an estimated $3.6bn owed to creditors and a $20m lifeline required from lenders to ward off liquidation.
Super giants have an indirect exposure to the beleaguered property developer through loans they have made to Bathla lenders such as Centuria Capital or Hong Kong investment house PAG.
The $115bn construction industry fund Cbus said it was selective about its lending in the Australian private market and would allocate its dollars elsewhere if that made better sense.
Cbus, a client of property fund manager Centuria Capital which owns private credit business Centuria Bass, had nothing to say about that exposure. Centuria Bass this month froze $670m of investor money in two of its funds exposed to Bathla.
“The rise of private credit businesses that want to build their funds under management, often through products offered to private wealth and SMSF investors, means that there is competition in the market for business and deals that once would not have been done. That’s not a space we operate in,” chief investment officer Leigh Gavin said.
“Cbus has always taken a selective approach to lending opportunities, and we will continue to do so to ensure any debt investments make sense on a return-for-risk basis for our members.
“If we can’t find good opportunities in the credit space domestically, we can consider managers globally. If credit is not the right place to put the next marginal dollar, we can always look at allocations to other asset classes – we don’t have to force the issue.” Australian Super and ART declined to comment. The $370bn ART has directed tens of millions of dollars to PAG.
Hostplus chief executive David Elia said he was more cautious of the local private credit market as headwinds grew.
“Private credit isn’t the problem, poorly underwritten credit is the problem. And a tougher interest-rate environment has a habit of revealing the difference,” he said. “That said, we are certainly more cautious today. Australian private credit has grown very quickly and we are now entering an environment that will provide a genuine test of underwriting standards across the sector.” Higher interest rates would heap pressure on highly leveraged borrowers and expose managers relying more heavily on benign credit conditions and rising asset values, he added.
Inflation data released last week has lifted expectations that interest rates are on the rise, a move that would heap pressure on segments of the private lending sector, property development in particular.
The expected push higher in interest rates comes as a housing slump takes hold in the wake of the federal government’s changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax.
“We would expect defaults and impairments to rise from very low levels, particularly in more leveraged and property related parts of the market and we think investors should be increasingly discerning about where and with whom they deploy capital,” Mr Elia said.
In a sign of the lack of depth in Australia’s private credit market, which is heavily skewed toward property development, both UniSuper and Colonial First State said there were better private credit opportunities offshore than at home.
“Our private credit strategy is focused offshore, targeting the upper middle markets of the US and Europe,” CFS CIO Jonathan Armitage said.
“We favour large and established businesses with strong cash flows and business models, and meaningful scale.
“There are a range of reasons for these strategic exposures, with one of the advantages being the in-built resilience that often comes with businesses of institutional quality.
“While there are attractive opportunities domestically, we believe larger global markets provide broader opportunities across industries and geographies, and a compelling mix of diversification, return and resilience for our members.” The corporate regulator this week warned Bathla Group’s failure was “the first real test for private credit”. “We’ve been talking about this and calling out what we see as some of these risks for a long time,” ASIC chair Sarah Court said. “I think unfortunately what we’re seeing at the moment – and it is early days, and no doubt more and more information will come out in the weeks and months that come – but what we’re seeing is in Australia the first significant cracks.”
